Could I urge you very much, Ms. Hasan, to ask, as I said before, important questions and not the obvious ones as what do you see on the photograph? I see a scattered glass. Because that's the kind of things the Chamber can see itself as well. We take a break and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I raise the following matter. By an informal communication on the 13th of February, the Prosecution has submitted a request to use a comments charge with Witness Anton Brennskaag, RM108, in relation to four non-associated exhibits. The Chamber notes that the request relates to four documents and does not object to using a chart. However, should the OTP wish to tender these four documents into evidence, the Chamber notes that they amount to in excess of 80 pages in total and urges the Prosecution to make a careful selection of what it seeks to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And yes. One remaining matter, but let's first focus again on the testimony of this witness. Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just trying to find the transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, you were questioned by the Honourable Judge Orie based upon what the witnesses told you, and at temporary transcript page 47, lines -- lines 20 through 23, or thereabouts, you said something about since the projectiles were fired from not a far distance you could hear the shell being fired and then an explosion where it landed. Did you also have occasion to hear from people that they either heard or saw the round or shell in flight? If could you clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now I'd like to focus about the time that you left the on-site investigation, headed to the hospital to perform your portion of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can follow along P957, MFI, is the prior testimony under Rule 92 ter. Page 5 of the same should be correlating to T6812 of the Galic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And lines 18 through 25 should be the part where you are talking about the hospital. There you go. And the question asked, sir, is as follows: "Q. When you went to the hospital, what did you do in respect to this task of trying to identify the dead and the injured? "A. In the admissions department of the Kosevo Hospital, the records are kept of all the persons who had -- had been admitted to the hospital, so the full name of the person admitted is recorded, the time of admission, as well as other personal details. And these records enabled me to determine the number of patients that had been admitted to the Kosevo Hospital in the time-period after the explosion at the Markale market. After that, I went to the morgue and there, on the bases of the documents that I had gathered from the personnel in the morgue, I verified..." And then you go on on the next page to describe what you verified. What I want to ask you about, sir, is this seems to imply that you went and reviewed the admissions records on the first day before you went to the morgue. Is that, in fact, accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we arrived at the hospital, we first established what the list of persons admitted to the hospital was. It was a list of persons that they had registered in their admissions records.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know approximately what time it is that you arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived after the on-site investigation. I can't tell you what time it was with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can have 1D789 up in e-court. Page 2 in both versions. This is, again, the 2001 statement of the witness. And I'm confused because, sir, the statement you gave seems to indicate the opposite, that you went to the morgue first, but I'd like to present that to you and get your comment on it. So we're looking at page 2 in both versions, the first full paragraph on the English version. Whoops. Sorry, the third full -- the fourth paragraph. It says: "I then went to the morgue at Kosevo Hospital, Sarajevo, with the team. There were four rooms full of bodies and I could see that they were mainly older men and women. I met with workers and employees at the morgue, and they were searching the bodies and trying to find papers or documents which could identify the people who had been killed." And if we skip to the last couple of lines of this paragraph, it says: "I remained at the morgue for approximately two hours that day. I think approximately 60 people were confirmed dead at Kosevo Hospital. Some people died later from their injuries and more bodies were brought from other hospitals." Now, according to this, you went to the morgue the first day. Can you help us here? Which -- which is accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- let's -- let's try, Mr. Ivetic, to -- Is there anywhere that the witness in this statement says that he first went to the morgue and then to the admission department? Because then there may be a contradiction. From what I read, but I'm reading it now in a second only, I only see that the witness here says that he went to the morgue and did not say that he went after that or that he went before that to any other department of the hospital. So if you are seeking to -- clarification, fine. No problem. But not in terms of which of the two is true and then not contradicting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought I'd asked for clarification because the statements starts -- the last line [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I said you could proceed and you ask him which of the two, isn't it? If you really insist. The question was: "Which is accurate?" That suggests a contradiction which I have not found. You may proceed, and we'll listen to your next question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm for us whether, in fact, you went to the morgue the first day or did you view the admissions records the first day? Or both? Or neither? Please help me.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The morgue and the admissions department are situated on the same wing of the Kosevo Hospital. I can tell you with certainty that I was both at -- in the admissions department and the morgue. It can be assumed that I first went to the admissions department and then to the morgue, though I can't vouch for that. It's been a long time. What I can confirm with certainty is that I visited both these departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm this part of your statement where it says: "I remained at the morgue for approximately two hours that day"?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how long I stayed there. What I know was that the whole fact-finding effort took two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have any reason to believe that when you gave this statement that you signed an affirmation for in December 2001, that, when you said you spent approximately two hours in the morgue, that your memory was clearer and better on that day than it is today?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in the admissions department reviewing the records of the hospital on that first day, the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to your Rule 92 ter testimony, P957, MFI, and page 7 of the same, that should correlate to transcript page 6814 of the underlying transcript. And I'd like lines 1 through 4 of the same. And, sir, again, I have to translate this for you since do not have a Serbian or Bosnian translation. "Q. How long did you remain at the Kosevo Hospital on the 5th of February, 1994? "A. On that day, I remained there for two hours. About two hours in the Kosevo Hospital." Now, sir, and I put it to you that if you spent a total of about two hours at the Kosevo Hospital, and your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2001 says that you spent approximately two hours at the morgue, that could you not have spent any significant amount of time in the admissions Department of Kosevo Hospital on the same day, as the time would eclipse two hours. Are you perhaps willing to concede that the admissions department was viewed by yourself at some point in time after the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not willing to concede that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When were the post mortems performed as to the bodies that were at the Kosevo Hospital, at the morgue?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when the post mortems were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you present when the pathologist examined the bodies and confirmed the cause of death as being shrapnel wounds?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Dobraca and I, together, carried out the identification of the bodies for whom we had no evidence of identity. Through the local radio station, we launched an appeal to all the persons who knew their family members were missing to come to the morgue for identification purposes. So Dr. Dobraca and I were there receiving these individuals who were coming to the morgue to confirm that they knew some of the victims. Because some of the victims were terribly disfigured, Dr. Dobraca would ask the family members or friends coming whether the individual had undergone an appendix surgery or something like that, and if the answer was affirmative, then we were able to establish that it was, indeed, a relative of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm confused. My question asked about examinations of the bodies. Were you present for any post mortems performed by Dr. Dobraca on the bodies or at the hospital morgue relating to the Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not present for the post mortems.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I would ask to you please explain page 9 of your Rule 92 ter transcript, which correlates to transcript page 6816 -- well, first of all, if we can start from the prior page, line 23 of the prior page which would be 6815, which would be page 8 of P957, MFI. And, again, sir, you'll have to follow along with me. It says here, beginning at line 23. "Q. Very well. Now, on the 6th of February, 1994, did you observe any proceedings carried out on the bodies of the deceased? "A. All the persons who had been killed were examined by the pathologist, and he carried out an expert examination of the bodies in order to determine the cause of death. And every person that was brought into the Kosevo Hospital, the cause of death was determined and records were kept of the proceedings. "Q. Were you present when these examinations were conducted? "A. I was present in most of the cases but I don't remember whether I was present during the examination [sic] of all those who had been killed. But I had the relevant documents by the pathologist confirming the cause of death for all those persons, specifying that they were all killed by shell shrapnel." Is this portion of your Rule 92 ter testimony accurate, or do you wish to change it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This portion of my testimony was either mistranslated or misinterpreted. It relates, I believe, to my work with Dr. Dobraca on identifying these victims. We spent together the total of two days establishing the identity of individuals. At the time, Dr. Dobraca was dealing with those individuals whose identity could not be established, showing the body and establishing the causes of death. I did not, however, participate in his special, technical examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to take a brief look at 1D789. That's, again, the 2001 statement. Page 1 in both languages. And the second paragraph from the bottom in both languages. And I would read for you as follows. You could follow along, sir, in the Bosnian version. The second paragraph from the bottom begins: "I returned to Kosevo Hospital again on the 6th February 1994. We continued the process of trying to identify the bodies. Friends and relatives came and we went to each body trying to identify them. I met with Dr. Ilijas Dobraca who was the pathologist on duty. He examined the bodies in my presence and confirmed the cause of death in each case as a result of shrapnel wounds. Some of the bodies had dreadful injuries." Is this portion of your 2001 statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is. Let me just add: It was quite evident that the cause of death was shrapnel. As he was walking through the morgue, Dr. Dobraca explained all these injuries were the result of -- of an explosion. Now when he was writing down his findings, that's something that I didn't have any part in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I -- at this point in time, put a question to the witness. Can you describe the method Dr. Dobraca used in your presence examining the bodies? How did he do that; and was that different or identical with post mortem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't say that Dr. Dobraca conducted the actual post mortem in my presence. He would approach each and every one of the victims and say, you see, this is the effect of shrapnel. If the body is headless or something like that, then obviously it could not have been the result of gun-fire. So we went from body to body, and he would explain to me that the cause of death was shrapnel. His official report, when he was producing an official report on autopsies, that's not something that I participated in. We were walking around the morgue, looking at the various bodies, and he was telling me that all these people had died as a result of shrapnel wounds, and he was showing me, in fact, what sort of effect shrapnel can produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for clarifying this matter. Now, I'd like to return back to your 92 ter testimony. P957, MFI. And this will be at page 14, which should be transcript page 6821, lines 5 through 25. I don't think I have to read the whole thing for you. I think you can see there, sir, the -- the numbers 142 and 67. Here it is recorded that you determined and reported that 67 lives were lost and 142 people incurred injuries. And I want to ask you, first of all, with regard to these figures, can you confirm the bases, the totality of the bases that these figures are based upon? What records, indeed, were reviewed to come to these totals.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When determining these figures, we used the figures we received from the Kosevo Hospital, the State Hospital, the UNPROFOR headquarters. These sources I can cite with certainty as having been the ones that we based our figures on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mention the UN headquarters. Was there a significant amount of information from the UN headquarters, or was the primary focus the hospital records of the State Hospital, on the one hand, and the Kosevo Hospital, on the other?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We received one piece of information from the UN headquarters. I think it was in the PTT building because several injured persons had been transported there. There were dead persons as well, if I remember correctly, but I don't know what the exact numbers were of either the dead persons or injured persons. I mean those who had been transported to the UNPROFOR headquarters and the UNPROFOR hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I forget if it was in your 92 ter statement or in your -- it's in the selection from the 2001 statement wherein you said: "I think approximately 60 people were confirmed dead at Kosevo Hospital." Would that imply that the majority of the casualties were derived from the review of the records of the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of the injured persons were transported to the Kosevo Hospital, and most information was received from the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can -- first of all, sir, isn't it true that due to the volume of persons that were coming in that the hospital staff did not enter data into the admission records for -- for the injured and deceased persons coming in from the Markale location at the time that they arrived, but, rather, entered the data throughout the day in batches when they had time; that is, after -- many times hours after the people arrived? Did you discover that when you reviewed the documents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now that I established that, nor whether I had such knowledge. The situation was unusual and extraordinary, and it is perhaps possible that not everything was done according to the normal procedure. But this is something I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how much time you spent going over the hospital admissions records in terms of was it significant, was it brief? Was it alone or with the assistance of somebody? Any further information you can give us as to the process by which you examined the hospital records to determine and find the identities and numbers of persons that were killed and injured?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is the question related to the 5th of February only or the couple of days --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The entirety of his investigation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the question was about how many time approximately you spent going through the hospital admission records, not exclusively on the 5th but during your investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't say now how much time was used to check the hospital records. I know for sure that the process of establishing the identity of persons lasted two or three days on the whole. And it wasn't just me who took part in that but my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to take a look at 65 ter number 10458. And when that comes up on the screen, I'd like to look at the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could look at the -- if you could look at the one in the original language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And perhaps for purposes, if we can have just have the original language up on the screen and enhanced so that the witness could have the best opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this, can you recognise or confirm for us that this is the type of hospital records that you would have reviewed of the Sarajevo Clinical Centre reception and triage block?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had before me the records from the Kosevo Hospital. But I cannot claim with certainty that these were the records because I cannot see the hospital's stamp anywhere here. Which does not exclude the possibility that these are the records, because judging by the rubrics it seems to me that this was what I examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go on the second page, I think the second page has a stamp. In the original. That's a little bit better. Do you recognise that stamp, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly. That is the stamp from the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we return to the first page of this document in the original. And it would be, I think, page 4, unfortunately, in the translation. And if we look at entry number 705, will you agree with me, sir, based on the date and time of this entry that this would be the first potential victim from the Markale incident that came to the Kosevo Hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, is it your understanding, sir, that the Markale incident occurred sometime after noon on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this entry shows the individual came in at 12.35 on that date.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that the individuals before are all dated at 8.00 in the morning and 10.00 in the morning and that therefore they can be excluded from the Markale group. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at 699, I see something that looks like 1635 or something like that. And 698, I see 12-something. 701, I see 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And if you look at the top of the page, that's the 4th of February 1994 and the -- starting at line 701 is the 5th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to page 7 in the B/C/S and it's going to be page 22 in the English. I apologise. The translation is much different from the original pages. And if we can look at entry 777 for a Hodzic Fikret. Do you see that all the other entries around are at 1235 and his is at 15 hours, and I believe, 45 minutes in the original. Although I think the English might have had 15 minutes. In any event, that this individual was received three hours after the approximate time of the Markale explosion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I don't see the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the English, again, it's page 22. And it should be the bottom entry. And -- oh, it does 1545. I had it wrong in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we exclude this individual, number 777, from being part of the group of persons brought in from Markale based upon the time? Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say because I don't know on what basis this patient showed up at the hospital. Did he sustain slight injuries and came to hospital himself? Or whether he sustained any injuries in some other place, this is something that I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can -- do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that the following numbers are back at 1235 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, apparently the sequence of registration may not be the same as the sequence of being brought to the hospital. Because I see 778 is again 1235.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whether this one we have no explanation as yet, and the witness has not given any at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, the question I guess following up on what the Honourable Judge has mentioned, would this not indicate to you that the hospital admissions records were being written at a later time, i.e., not at 1235 but at some later time when the hospital staff found time to enter this information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic [sic] it's so -- Mr. Ivetic, it's so obvious. If I have five pages in the same handwriting with 1235, to assume that that all could have been written in one minute is, of course, out of my imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the witness said that he examined the admissions records when he first arrived. If they weren't written, how could he have do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't know when it was down. Whether it was at 1240, 1200. We do not know exactly. The witness doesn't remember exactly when it happened. Let's try to avoid a quasi-accuracy which may not be in line with reality, and the Chamber is primarily interested to know what happened in reality. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could -- if we could turn to -- if we could turn to page 9 in the original B/C/S and page 27 in the English, at item number 795, we see an individual Keso, Bisma, admitted at 1610 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether you included her in the count of Markale injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean injured? Or dead or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Injured or dead. At this point I'm just asking for the total count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do remember, answer the question. If you don't remember, tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this person Bisma, Keso, I couldn't say whether she was on the list or injured and so on and so forth. I do not remember the name and I cannot say with any precision how many casualties either injured or dead there were at the moment. But I stand by the information included in the official report and the criminal report which I wrote later on because I believe that that information is correct and authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at this page, the last entry that has the 1235 marking is item 797, entry 797, with all the subsequent entries being 17 and 1800 hours, would you be able to confirm that entry number 797 is likely the last Markale-related entry in this hospital admission log-book?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this document at this time into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at number 9998 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when that comes up, sir, I'll ask again to focus on the original language version, the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I meanwhile ask another question. Witness, could you tell us when you went to the admission department, what they had written down there as admitted patients, was that already in its final format or - that means written in the books - or would there have been notes to then later to be entered into the official records? Do you have any recollection of what you found there? If you have, please tell us; if you don't have, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, Your Honours, on my arrival to the Kosevo Hospital, the first thing I found there was a big upheaval, running around, panic, patients coming from all sides. In many instances the dead were directly transported to the morgue. Those who were injured were brought to departments and so on. So the service did not operate normally and sometimes if they contacted them from a specific department and said the patient reached us, they would then enter him in the protocol, so I'm sure that under such extraordinary circumstances they could not observe any type of rules for registering the incoming patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at the first page of this document, sir, in the original language, do you recognise it and can confirm that this is the -- appears to be the admissions book for the records of the State or Military Hospital in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not examine the books of the State Hospital, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we are looking at P706, MFI'd, at this moment, which is the same as 65 ter 9998. Please proceed. This is just for those who are reading the record later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I did not realise that it'd already been used in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How did you obtain the information from the State or Military Hospital if you did not look at the admissions records for the same in reaching your total determination of the totality of the injured and -- the injured and the deceased from this incident that you were investigating?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember with certainty how we obtained the information, but there were two possible ways. Either one of my colleague was there, examined it, and then submitted the report to me, or the hospital submitted a report on these persons who were admitted and who had been injured or killed, and they would have submitted such a report at our request. We followed the same procedure as regards the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at entry number 851 which should be at the top of the page that is on the screen now. Would the time and date for this incident be consistent with this individual being an entry for a Markale-related victim? Again, as I read it, it's the 5th of February, 1994, and if we zoom in under the patient name, I believe -- well, now I can't be certain if that's the time or something else. That could also be something else. Do you see the date at least on the left, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the 5th of February, 1994. I could not say anything about this because I'm not familiar with the document as such. So if this person is listed here, then it was probably established that this was a person injured or killed at the Markale market and then transported to the State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Since it is MFI'd, I think we do need to go through some items that I did not note on the English translation that do exist on the B/C/S original. If we can look at the third page in B/C/S and the second page in English, I think this one is okay. I think that on both we have a cross out of the -- of the item on the top, number 856. Yes, it's crossed out. So that one is okay. If we look at page 9 in the B/C/S and page 6 in the English, and I think the entries at 879 and 880 in the original are crossed off but are not so denoted on the translation. Can you confirm, sir, based upon your review of other hospital records, did any staff ever explain to you what it meant when entries were crossed off on these types of ledgers or books that they kept? If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not records from the Kosevo Hospital, as far as I can remember. And I already said that I did not examine the records from the State Hospital, so I cannot provide an explanation for anything that has been crossed out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the State Hospital as part of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- as far as I remember, I did not go to the State Hospital during the investigation. I didn't go there personally, but it's possible that some of my colleagues did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, for the attention of the parties and Chamber, I believe at page 11 in B/C/S and 7 in English, item number 882 is another entry that is crossed or scratched off where the English translation does not denote the entirety of that answer. I bring that everyone's attention since it is a MFI'd document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Prosecution seek that the translation will be reviewed so that crossed out portions are indicated as such also in English. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the totality of these two documents together, I went through all the entries, and according to my math, we could come up with only 39 deceased individuals and 120 wounded individuals. I looked at the photographs that were taken as part of the -- the -- the investigation, and I note that there are 39 photographs of 39 deceased individuals. Where are the photographs of the remaining fatalities from this investigation that would have been taken pursuant to the standard operating procedure that you testified about earlier that would have been followed for the Markale investigation?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot provide an explanation for the part of my work for which the forensic officers were in charge. I can say that when I visited the morgue, when touring the four rooms of the morgue, I found around 60 bodies at the morgue. It's probable that the families of the deceased took over the bodies of their relatives from the morgue and so the photographer was unable to make those photographs. But this is just an assumption. I cannot really give an explanation of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At Exhibit P868, there's a document dated the 5th of February, 1994, and it appears at pages 22 and 23 of both versions of that exhibit that identifies named and unknown fatalities as to the incident, and that document identifies 41 dead individuals. Is this a document that you had access to and that you relied upon in doing your own investigation and reaching your determination of 67 fatalities?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of fatalities kept growing because there were people who had been transported alive but who then died during transportation or on being admitted to the hospital. And then they were sent back downstairs to the morgue, and, therefore, the number of fatalities kept growing per hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that on the 8th of February, 1994, the CSB documented 69 dead, whereas your final tally, authored on the 17th of February, 67 are dead. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information is collected until the moment when investigation is ended and a criminal report is being drafted. So the information may be changed if new facts are determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We could take the break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber wonders, are -- is this line of questioning, is this about imperfection of registration and mistakes and flaws in what happened on that day, or is this a basis for a suggestion that it was fraudulent and it was all staged? In which case, I think it would be fair to put that to the witness. Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this stage, I'm examining the witness to give facts and to allow the Chamber to make that determination. I'm more than happy to put it to the witness that there was pressure on the CSB from the Sarajevo authorities to inflate the numbers. I can -- I would be more than happy to put that to the witness. That was my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it inflation of numbers or the whole thing being staged and fraudulently presented?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness only dealt with the identification of the victims and therefore I believe that it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you what the Defence's case is in this respect, because it would be fair -- if you elicit evidence from a witness in support of the Defence's case, then I think that it is appropriate to put to that witness what the Defence case is in that respect. That's what the Rule requires. Would you please think this over during the break. We'll take a break, and we will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time. I started with the request of the 13th of February earlier. In that same e-mail, there also is a request to add associated exhibits that the Prosecution had omitted from its Rule 92 ter motion and is still in relation to Witness RM108, and the Prosecution should request any relief it seeks on the record when the witness testifies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber appreciate if you would be able to finish in, well, let's, say, 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is my plan, Your Honour, and hopefully I can do it without the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I put it to you that there was a great deal of pressure on the CSB personnel performing the investigation into this Markale incident from the BiH government authorities to manipulate and inflate the numbers of casualties for this incident in order to support the propaganda that was being presented to seek intervention against the Serbs. Would you agree or concede any portion of that based upon your experiences?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have pressure put upon me on -- of this sort in my line of work, nor was my impression that my work colleagues were under any such pressure. The aim we had was to collect as much evidence and facts in as short a period of time, and any pressure other than this one can be fully ruled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move onto the last part of my examination dealing with the incident at Marin Dvor that you also testified about, the sniping incident you said with the trams yesterday. And I'd like to ask you, first of all, at this trial we've had evidence, specifically at transcript page 5870, from an UNPROFOR official by the name of David Fraser relating to other incidents in this same general area that are from February of 1994, so a few months after the incident in question. And at that time it was determined that the trams were hit by machine-gun fire that was found to be the result of a fire-fight between Serb and Muslim forces that were located 300 metres away. At the time that you were conducting the investigation into the incident in October of 1994 -- I apologise, I misspoke. When I was talking about February, it was February of 1995. The incident that you investigated was in October of 1994. Did you at that time have information as to the positions of the combatant forces and how near they were to the tram line so as to determine if there had been any combat or exchange of fire during the date when the incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information about positions is something that I had. This sort of information was available to all citizens because it was commonly known that across from the Miljacka river there were positions held by the VRS, whereas on the other bank of the Miljacka, on the right bank, there were BH army positions. This line of confrontation was, I'm not sure, but roughly 300 metres away from the tram line in question. As far as I remember now, trams were operational only at times when there were cease-fires in force. They weren't operational at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, yesterday you were shown a photograph of the one deceased individual. Am I correct that his entry wound was on the right side of his head and the exit wound was on the left side at the shoulder-blade level?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when the post mortem was carried out of this body, and the only thing I had was the photograph that was taken by the photographer at the time that was sent to me by the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at P493 and not broadcast the same, as it is under seal. And page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is the report that was, I believe, viewed yesterday with you. And did you have occasion -- looking at the first page, do you -- do you recall this -- this report that you looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can look at page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S, dealing with the deceased person, it is in the text stated that the deceased person is identified, it says: "He had died from a perforating wound to the right part of his head where the entry wound is located, while the exit wound is on his left shoulder-blade." Now does that refresh your recollection that this was a fact that was determined by the investigation that you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is an established fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now based on your knowledge and experience investigating incidents and perhaps a little bit of logic, doesn't this seem to indicate to you that the shooter was shooting downwards at him from a closer distance as opposed to a distance further away?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my logic and experience at that time, my conclusion would be that the fire had been opened from some distance higher up because the bullet entered the head and exited at the shoulder level, indicating that fire had been opened from a higher position, and this is something that we experienced in sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to the surroundings of the tram line, did you in fact investigate to determine if any higher positions in the vicinity could have been manned by any units of the BiH forces that could have been the source of the shot?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area where the incident took place, there are no elevations. There are only buildings. Sky-scrapers on both sides of the Miljacka. On the left bank of the Miljacka, which was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, I know for a fact - and it was generally known - that there were Serbian sniper units in the Metalka building. May I conclude --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have to -- I have to interrupt because my question was very specific and I have very little time. Did you investigate buildings manned by the BiH forces that were in an elevated position; i.e., higher -- high rise buildings surrounding the tram line on the BiH side? Did your investigation look into those buildings to exclude them as the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that some UN personnel on the scene actually reported that the fire came from one of these buildings as opposed to from the other side of the river?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't investigate the buildings surrounding the scene of the incident, and according to my information UNPROFOR did not take any actions to establish what the state effects was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could take a look at the first page of this document that's still up on the screen in e-court. And I'd like to read the first paragraph of the actual report that starts: "This Centre ..." "This centre was informed by the duty operative at 1245 hours on 08 October 1994 that in Marin Dvor in Centar municipality, near the building of the museum, fire was opened from the aggressor's positions which are on the Grbavica PZT against trams that were transporting passengers." Can we confirm from this official report that at the time that the investigative team was sent to the scene, the CSB had already predetermined that the source of fire were the aggressor forces at the Grbavica PZT?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report was sent to the chief, and I did inform the chief about my knowledge about this event. It was the assumption of the forensic technicians that that was the direction of fire, and I included that information in my report and informed the chief of the CSB about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I just want to say receiving information is one thing. Predetermination is quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And this, I believe, is at the time that the team hasn't even been out to the site yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have just received information. The sentence says the center was informed by the duty operative. That's the information they have. Now they are going to investigate that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to page 2 in the English and stay on page 1 in the B/C/S. I'd like to see exactly where the information came from and at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The part that I am interested in starts with the name Milos, Vjekoslav, son of Ferdinand, and mother Marija, born 11 April 1955 in Sarajevo, was the driver of tram number 206, which had been shot at. He permanently resides at 11 Bozidar Adzic -- Adzije Street. He stated that: "Burst fire was opened against the tram at about 1219 hours and that the aggressor soldiers probably fired from the Grbavica PZT, that is, from the building known as Metalka."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Too fast, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So the pertinent part here is that the tram driver said that he thought, believed, that the aggressor soldiers probably fired from the Grbavica PZT. It is this the bases for the conclusion by your team that in fact the source of fire was this Metalka building?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, these are all facts and statements that we took in the course of the investigation and the official opinion was given by the forensics team who had examined the scene to see what -- where the projectile had arrived from. And the driver here was probably relating his feeling that the projectile had come from that direction. It was probably on the basis of this statement that we received news of fire having been opened from Metalka and that we should attend the scene to establish what the actual state of facts was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your investigation determine why this driver felt that the shots came from the Metalka building? Did he see muzzle flashes?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to explain this. In this area, on the side --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to know what your investigation found out from this driver of this tram. What is the bases for his position that the fire came from Metalka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. First of all, please calm down. That's one. Second, I think the witness explained that they noticed that the driver said that he thought, believed, that it was probably fired from there and there. If the witness -- if the driver would have said, I saw the flashes of the muzzle, of course, the evidence would be entirely different. Then the witness further explained that it apparently was an impression by the driver. And then to ask these kind of questions do not help. It's clear that it was a subjective impression by the driver which was at the basis of the report. Now, that may be important for the Defence, but then to follow up and to say, Did he see any muzzle flashes? That seems not to be assisting the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to found out what the witness's bases is for his statement earlier that the forensic guys determined from where the fire is coming from. If they are relying upon the bus driver and that's the bases of their examination, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He doesn't know apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could use then, perhaps, the last few minutes you have. You put to the witness that at page - which one was it? - at page 5870, testimony of Mr. Fraser, that the testimony he gave: "... that it was determined that the trams were hit by machine-gun fire that was found to be the result of a fire-fight between Serb and Muslim forces that were locate the 300 metres away." Could you please indicate to me where on that page this conclusion can be found?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Lines 1 through 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which says that, at the same time, there was exchange of fire. I do not read in any way that the projectile that hit the tram was determined to be part of that exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Line number 14: "During the same time-period both sides were involved in a fire-fight 300 metres away in the area of the Vrbanja Bridge (BP 912589). An MG CFV has been attributed to both the BiH and BSA for the event overall."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this witness, Mr. Fraser was questioned upon that, and this is one of the incidents that was dropped from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, my simple question is: Where in this page it is said that the bullet that hit the tram was part of that exchange of fire? Because that is what you put to the witness. And the only thing I see is that there was an exchange of fire and that a registered violation of a cease-fire agreement was established for both sides, which means both sides apparently fired in violation of a cease-fire agreement. It doesn't say anything about the bullet that hit the tram was part of this exchange of fire, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd have to go back and look at the underlying document number 1096, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You said it was found on page 5870. That's where I looked and that's where I do not find it, and you're invited to next time to specifically read the line you are referring to in order to avoid such kind of difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I add something. On page 5870, in e-court, in the question there's a quotation from a previous testimony, probably of this witness, but the witness didn't answer any question on that page. Only the very short one at the end: "Yes, it says a machine-gun cease-fire violation." This is the only answer of that witness recorded on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I was going to raise this matter later, but since we're on the topic, the -- Mr. Ivetic put on the record that David Fraser referred -- there was incidents that occurred in February 1995. On -- that were shown to David Fraser and discussed with him. In fact, he was shown one document relating to a single incident that occurred in February 1995. So I just wanted that correction to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic you may conclude in the next three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You yesterday talked about the forensic examination that determined that the bullet that caused the fatality may have been from the death sower. What investigations did you undertake to determine if armija BiH forces on the side of the confrontation line closer to the tram had a death sower in their inventory? And where would we look to find those investigative efforts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first simple question is whether you have any knowledge whether the BiH forces had death sowers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I supposed that they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any specific knowledge or you supposed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, while I was serving the army in Stup, I could see some soldiers who had these sowers of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question now is: Did you make part of your investigation whether the fire by the death sower may have come from BiH positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We excluded that aspect from our investigation for the reason that the ballistic experts determined the incoming trajectory of the projectiles which did not include any indications suggesting that it could have got there from the positions of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would it be the standard operating procedure of the CSB Sarajevo to fully document any such investigations including any forensic findings?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our investigation, we certainly used the findings and opinion of experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question was a bit different. Was it standard operating procedure of the CSB Sarajevo to fully document in writing the investigative steps and any forensic findings?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Ms. Hasan, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have one question. But before I do so, yesterday when we discussed the admission of the 92 ter transcript, I understood from Your Honour that there -- the Defence may have an opportunity to tender portions of the cross-examination after the completion of the testimony, and I think I need to get the Defence's position before I re-direct, because if there are any portions that are included now, then I would have to assess them to see if there's any questions arising from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As matters stand now, the Defence has referred to a few portions being read out literally to the witness and they did not tender any other portions of the transcript. Therefore, the Chamber assumes, at this moment, that the Defence does not tender any additional portions --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and only will rely on portions read out literally.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: At page 20 to 22 of today's transcript, my friend Mr. Ivetic asked you questions about media reports, newspaper reports that you had read regarding the existence of Seve Units, et cetera. I take it, Witness, that would you -- well, my question is, would you be in a position to comment on the truthfulness or accuracy of those media reports that you read?

utterances.speaker: EDIN SULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to say anything specific about this event because I did not know anything about this while I performed my duties as an inspector in the war crimes and genocide department. The manipulation of these -- of this information began after the war, after I had transferred to the civilian authorities. My position to such information is that I receive it with some reserve, because if I may say so before this Tribunal, this information is used in order to achieve certain goals in the conflicts between various political parties. So I accept the information but with a certain amount of mistrust. And if I may add, even if they are true, I would say that these units were primarily used for the purposes of internal settling of accounts within the ranks of the BH army and police, rather than to liquidate the Serbian population, as this is sometimes claimed in the media. And that is my personal position about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for answering all of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no further questions. Mr. Ivetic, has the one question by the Defence -- by the Prosecution triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It has not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has not. Then, this concludes your evidence, Mr. Suljic, your evidence in this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I hope that you'll have a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I use -- yes, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to follow up on a number of outstanding issues from the examination of this witness; mainly, the transcript, the proffered 92 ter transcript has not yet been admitted. It's been MFI'd. That's P957, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, the translation issue is standing, that remains or?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As a matter of fact, from the examination of the witness, I think we've realised at least two or three-points that the printed transcript or what is said the witness said is incorrect, so I think that it needs to be addressed whether it's a transcription error or what, but there was at least the one part where he said it was wrong, and then I presented him the -- the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has listened to it in his own language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and -- but he hasn't been able to follow the transcript because he can't follow the English transcript. He can only listen to the B/C/S. He has no way of knowing how it's recorded on the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that point. We'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the Chamber wondered where there was a mistake. Was that a portion that you introduced or was it a portion that the Prosecution had introduced?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a portion of the Prosecution and I believe it was at page 6816 of the Rule 92 ter transcript, the testimony, which should be the -- I want to say it's the 12th page but I can't be certain. It's the ninth page in e-court, I believe, sir, where we're talking about the pathologist and he indicated that this text was either wrong or had been misinterpreted because that was not what he had said. I'm paraphrasing of course now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the post mortem area --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. The post mortems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the objections and we'll decide in due course. Ms. Hasan, any other matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, just in relation to that matter, as far as I can recall, the witness did clarify that point about whether he was present or not. And together -- his prior testimony obviously is going to go in together with what he said over the last two days. I'm not sure, I don't appreciate that there is any other reason why not to admit the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the objection, together with your submission at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But it would be helpful if Mr. Ivetic could draw our attention to a specific portion of today's transcript where the witness referred to a mistake in the transcript of the earlier case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, so as not to take more court time, I could informally advise the parties via e-mail once I locate that -- what the temporary and the permanent transcript reference is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If would you send the e-mail to Chamber's staff as well, then. Any other matter, Ms. Hasan? If not, I'd like to deliver the Chamber's ruling on the Defence motion regarding response time for Rule 94 bis witness Reynaud Theunens. The Chamber will now rule on the Defence motion to enlarge the time to respond to the Prosecution's Rule 94 bis notice with regard to Witness Theunens and that was a motion from the 7th of February. The Prosecution's response was received on the 14th of February. In its response, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that a corrected version of the Theunens report has been uploaded under 65 ter number 28612 which rectified the various mixed up pages and other errors detected by the Chamber as outlined in its oral statement of the 24th of January 2013 at transcript pages 7373 to 7374. With regard to the Defence's request for an extension of time to respond, the Prosecution opposes and submits that it would be assisted by a response of the Defence, especially with regard to information overlapping with accepted adjudicated facts that should be redacted and possible challenges to the report itself. Contrary to the Prosecution's submission, the Chamber is of the view that it is the Prosecution's sole responsibility to properly consider the Chamber's request of the 24th of January, 2013, which is to redact any overlap with adjudicated facts and consider the relevance of over 180 pages of the report. As requested, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to make a new filing pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules. If the Prosecution feels that it could be assisted in this endeavour by the Defence, the parties may consult between themselves without the involvement of the chamber. In light of the forgoing the Chamber grants the Defence motion and allows the Defence 30 days from the date of the Prosecution's re-filing of the Theunens report to file its response. And this concludes the Chamber's ruling on this matter. If there is nothing else at this moment, we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume on Monday, the 18th of February, 2013, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of February, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
